title: An Apologist Winsome and Sure, Caroline Ong's Math is Beautiful High Horse Example se-example
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart introduces his signature strategy for building student Value: becoming "An Apologist Winsome and Sure" for one's discipline. Breaking down the word's Greek roots, appo, "out from," and logos, "reason, speech," he defines an apologist teacher as one from whom explanations of a subject's meaning and worth continuously flow, like a bubbling fountain. He offers parallel examples across ELA, personal finance, and math teachers, then introduces a video of Caroline Ong delivering a "math is beautiful" mini-rant to her geometry students as the concrete illustration of the concept in action. He identifies two qualities that make Ong's example work: her reasoning is winsome, delivered with evident enjoyment, and sure, delivered with confidence, rather than defensive in the everyday sense of "apologist." The piece closes with a direct call to action: teachers should regularly and unapologetically rant about why their discipline is beautiful, making it the classroom norm rather than the exception.
points: Stuart's etymological breakdown of "apologist," appo-logos, reframes the concept from making excuses to a continuous outflow of reasons and meaning.
The strategy is illustrated with a real classroom video, Caroline Ong, rather than left as pure theory, giving teachers a concrete model to imitate.
Two named qualities, winsome (enjoyment) and sure (confidence), give teachers a specific, checkable standard for whether their value-talk is landing well.
The call to action is explicitly about frequency and normalization: value-rants should become the classroom default, not a rare special occasion.
quotes: My favorite method for cultivating Value in the hearts of your students for the work of your discipline is called "An Apologist Winsome and Sure.

A teacher who is an apologist, then, is someone from whom words about the meaning and reason of what you do in your class flow out. I picture a fountain that's ever bubbling with water, the nourishing stuff of life.

The ELA teacher who is an apologist for English language arts is like a bubbling brook; he's always nonchalantly crafting these "positive micro moments" in which the class gets to marvel at the wonders of language.
She's giving reasons for mathematics (from point 1:20 in the video until the end) — in other words, she's giving an appo-logos, an apologetic.
Go have a ball briefly ranting at times about how beautiful and lovely and powerful and cool your discipline is. Do this as often as you can.
